en: Thus have I heard: the Caṅkī Sutta, the ninety-fifth discourse in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Opāsāda.
There, near Opāsāda, the Blessed One stayed in the Devavana Sāla Grove to the north of Opāsāda.

Now at that time, the brahmin Caṅkī resided in Opāsāda, a place teeming with living beings, well-supplied with grass, timber, water, and grain—a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment.
The brahmin householders of Opāsāda heard: "Friends,
the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan,
while wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a great community of monks, has arrived at Opāsāda and is staying to the north of Opāsāda in the Devavana Sāla grove."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama has spread abroad:

“Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Having personally realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, by means of his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
"He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Opāsāda departed from Opāsāda in groups, in companies, and in crowds, heading north toward the Devavana Sal Grove.
Now at that time, the brahmin Caṅkī had gone up to the upper terrace for his midday rest.
He saw the brahmin householders of Opāsāda emerging from Opāsāda in groups and crowds, heading north toward the Devavana Sālavana grove.
Having seen them, he addressed his steward:
“Master Steward, why is it that the brahmin householders of Opāsāda have gone out from Opāsāda in groups and crowds, heading north toward the Devavana Sāla grove?
“There is, Master Caṅkī, a recluse named Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan.
While wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a great community of bhikkhus, he has arrived at Opāsāda and is staying in Opāsāda to the north.”
Near the city, in the divine grove, in the Sāla forest.
Now, concerning that venerable Gotama, this excellent report has spread abroad:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
“Therefore, we are going to see Master Gotama.
“In that case, my good steward, go to the brahmin householders of Opāsāda; having approached them, say this to the brahmin householders of Opāsāda:
‘Sirs, the brahmin Caṅkī says thus:’”
“May the honorable ones come, for the brahmin Caṅkī will also approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
“Very well, sir,” that steward replied to the brahmin Caṅkī. He then went to the brahmin householders of Opāsāda and, having approached them, said to the brahmin householders of Opāsāda:
“Sirs, the brahmin Caṅkī says this:”
“Gentlemen, please wait; the brahmin Caṅkī will also approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
Now at that time, about five hundred brahmins from various kingdoms were staying at Opāsāda on some business.
Those brahmins heard:
“It is said that the brahmin Caṅkī will approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
Then those brahmins went to where the brahmin Caṅkī was, and having approached him, they said this to the brahmin Caṅkī:
“Is it true, sir, that you will approach the ascetic Gotama to see him?”
“Indeed, sir, this is my thought:
‘I shall approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
“Do not, Master Caṅkī, approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.”
It is not fitting for the venerable Caṅkī to approach the ascetic Gotama to see him;
rather, it is the ascetic Gotama who ought to approach the venerable Caṅkī to see him.
For the venerable Caṅkī is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, unassailable and beyond reproach in matters of birth.
Furthermore, since Master Caṅkī is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors,
unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth, for this reason also Master Caṅkī is not worthy to approach the ascetic Gotama for a visit.
The ascetic Gotama is indeed worthy to come and visit the venerable Caṅki.
For the venerable Caṅki is wealthy, of great fortune and vast possessions...

[as above] ...the venerable Caṅki has mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, liturgical formulas, phonology, and etymology, as well as the histories as the fifth; he is a master of philology and grammar, and is fully proficient in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man... [as above] ...

For Master Caṅkī is handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing a Brahmā-like form and a Brahmā-like grace, and is of such noble appearance that one never tires of seeing him...
[as before] ... For Master Caṅkī is virtuous, possessed of the virtue of the elders, and endowed with the virtue of the elders... [as before] ...

For Master Caṅkī is a speaker of what is good, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, free from indistinctness, and capable of making the meaning known... [as before].
For Master Caṅkī is the teacher of many teachers; he teaches the mantras to three hundred young brahmins...
Master Caṅkī is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by King Pasenadi of Kosala...
Master Caṅkī is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by the brahmin Pokkharasāti.

For Master Caṅkī dwells at Opāsāda— a place teeming with beings, abundant in grass, timber, and water, rich in grain, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment.
Insofar as Master Caṅkī dwells at Opāsāda— a place teeming with beings, abundant in grass, timber, and water, rich in grain,
a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment— for this reason he does not deserve [to be compared to you].
"Sir Caṅkī should approach the ascetic Gotama to see him;
indeed, the ascetic Gotama deserves to approach Sir Caṅkī to see him.
When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī spoke thus to those brahmins:
“In that case, sirs, listen to me as well: it is we who ought to go to see that ascetic Gotama, and not that venerable Gotama who ought to come to see us.

For the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and his father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth.”
Furthermore, sir, since the ascetic Gotama is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side,
of pure descent for seven generations back, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth,
on this account also that venerable Gotama does not deserve to come to see us.
Rather, it is we who ought to approach the venerable Gotama for an audience.
For the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has gone forth having renounced vast quantities of bullion and gold, both that stored in the earth and that held above ground...

[and so on] ...The ascetic Gotama, sirs, though still young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth and in the prime of life, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness... [and so on].

"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth from the home life into homelessness, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, even though his parents did not desire it and wept with tearful faces...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is handsome, pleasing, and serene, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; he possesses a divine form and a divine grace, being of no mean appearance...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is virtuous, possessing the virtue of a noble one, the virtue of one skilled in wholesome states, and is endowed with wholesome virtue..."
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is eloquent, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is refined, distinct, flawless, and capable of making the meaning known...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a teacher of many teachers...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has exhausted sensual desire and is free from fickleness..."
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action and a proponent of efficacy; he holds no regard for evil among the brahmin class...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a high family, an unbroken lineage of kshatriyas...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a wealthy family, one of great riches and great possessions..."
"Indeed, sirs, people come from across kingdoms and across countries to inquire about the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, many thousands of deities have gone for refuge with their lives to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, such a glorious report concerning the ascetic Gotama has spread abroad:"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.
… [and so on] … “Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
… [and so on] … “Indeed, sir, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama. … [and so on] …
"Indeed, sirs, King Pasenadi of Kosala, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Opāsāda and is staying north of Opāsāda in the Sal Grove, the Devavana."
"Whatever recluses or brahmins come to our village territory, they are our guests.
Now, guests must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by us.
Since the recluse Gotama has arrived at Opāsāda and is staying north of Opāsāda in the Devavana Sāla grove, the recluse Gotama is our guest."
Furthermore, a guest is indeed to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by us.
For this reason, that venerable Gotama does not deserve to come to see us;
rather, we ourselves ought to go to see that venerable Gotama.
"Sir, I can master only so much of that Master Gotama’s praise, yet Master Gotama is not merely of such praise;
for Master Gotama possesses immeasurable praise.
Even if he were endowed with only one of those qualities, Master Gotama would not deserve to come to see us."
“Indeed, we ourselves ought to approach the venerable Gotama for an audience.
“In that case, sirs, let us all together approach the ascetic Gotama for an audience.
Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large company of brahmins, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was seated after having exchanged various polite and courteous greetings with very elderly brahmins.
At that time, there was a young brahmin student named Kāpaṭika, who was youthful, with a shaven head, sixteen years of age by birth.
He was a master of the three Vedas, including the glossaries (nighaṇṭu) and liturgical formulas (keṭubha), along with phonology (sakkharappabheda) and the fifth branch, history (itihāsa);
he was a philologist and a grammarian, and was thoroughly proficient in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man.
Seated in that assembly, he would interrupt the conversation from time to time while the most eminent Brahmins were consulting with the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One rebuked the young brahmin Kāpaṭika:
“Let the venerable Bhāradvāja not interrupt the conversation while the elder brahmins are deliberating.
Let the venerable Bhāradvāja wait for the conclusion of their discussion.”
When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said this to the Blessed One:
“May Master Gotama not dismiss the young man Kāpaṭika.
The young man Kāpaṭika is of good family; the young man Kāpaṭika is learned; the young man Kāpaṭika is wise.”
"The young brahmin Kāpaṭika is eloquent, and he is capable of conversing with Master Gotama on this matter.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“Surely there must be a discussion regarding the Threefold Veda in the young brahmin Kāpaṭika’s presence;
for that is why the brahmins are placing him at their head.
Then it occurred to the young brahmin Kāpaṭika:
“When the ascetic Gotama directs his gaze toward me, then I will question the ascetic Gotama.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the young brahmin Kāpaṭika, directed his gaze toward where the young brahmin Kāpaṭika was.
Then it occurred to the young brahmin Kāpaṭika:
“The ascetic Gotama is paying attention to me.
What if I were to ask the ascetic Gotama a question?
Then the young brahmin Kāpaṭika said this to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, regarding this ancient Vedic lore of the brahmins, handed down through the tradition of ‘thus it was’ and ‘so it has been,’ and established as a scriptural canon, the brahmins therein reach a definitive conclusion, saying:
‘Only this is true; all else is false.
What does Master Gotama say about this?”
“But then, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says:
‘I know this; I see this.
This alone is the truth; all else is false’?”
“No, Master Gotama.
“But, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single teacher among the brahmins, or even a teacher’s teacher, back as far as the seventh generation of teachers, who has said this:
‘I know this; I see this’?”
“Is it only this that is true, and everything else false?
“No indeed, Master Gotama.
“But what then, Bhāradvāja, as for those ancient brahmin seers who were the authors of the hymns, the makers of the hymns—”
Those for whom this ancient mantra-word has been chanted, proclaimed, and established in the past—
those brahmins who now sing it, recite it, repeat what was spoken, and teach what was taught, namely: Aṭṭhaka,
Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu.
They also said this:
“We know this; we see this.
Only this is true; any other view is false.”
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“In that case, Bhāradvāja, it seems there is not even a single brahmin among them who says:
‘I know this; I see this.’”
‘This alone is the truth, all else is vain’—not even a single teacher among the brahmins, nor a teacher’s teacher, nor anyone back as far as the seventh generation of teachers, has ever said:
‘I know this; I see this.’
‘This alone is true, all else is vain’—
even those ancient seers of the brahmins, the makers of the mantras, the proclaimers of the mantras,
whose ancient mantra-words are now chanted, proclaimed, and rehearsed by the brahmins today.
They repeat what has been spoken and recite what has been chanted, namely:
Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu; yet even they did not say:
"We know this; we see this."
‘Only this is true, anything else is worthless.
Bhāradvāja, it is just as if there were a file of blind men clinging to one another: the one in front does not see, the one in the middle does not see, and the one in the back does not see.

In the same way, Bhāradvāja, I think the speech of the brahmins turns out to be like a file of blind men—the one in front does not see, the one in the middle does not see, and the one in the back does not see.
“What do you think, Bhāradvāja, does the faith of the brahmins not thus become groundless?
“Indeed, Master Gotama, it is not only out of faith that the brahmins attend upon them; they also attend upon them out of oral tradition.”
“Previously, Bhāradvāja, you relied on faith; now you speak from hearsay.
There are, Bhāradvāja, these five things that have a twofold result in this very life.
Which five?
Faith, preference, oral tradition, reasoned reflection, and approval based on contemplation of views—
these five things, Bhāradvāja, have a twofold result even in this present life.
Moreover, Bhāradvāja, there may be something well-faithed in, yet it is empty, hollow, and false.
Even if one has not heard it oneself, yet it is real, true, and not otherwise;
furthermore, Bhāradvāja, it may be well-pleasing to one...
[and so on] ...or it may be just as one has heard it oneself... [and so on].
It is indeed well-considered … [and so on] … it is indeed well-reflected upon, yet it is empty, vain, and false;
or even if it is not well-reflected upon, it is nevertheless real, true, and not otherwise.
“Bhāradvāja, for a wise person who guards the truth, it is not sufficient here to arrive at a conclusion with a one-sided certainty, thinking:
‘Only this is true; anything else is false.
“But in what way, Master Gotama, is there the guarding of the truth? In what way does one guard the truth?”
“We ask Master Gotama about the preservation of truth.
“Bhāradvāja, if a person has faith, [he thinks]:
‘Such is my faith.’”
Speaking thus, one protects what is true, yet one does not yet reach a definitive conclusion by way of a single side, thinking:
"Only this is true; anything else is false.
(*...*) If, Bhāradvāja, a person has a preference (*ruci*), (*...*) [and so on].
If, Bhāradvāja, a person has oral tradition … [as before] … if,
Bhāradvāja, a person has reasoned reflection … [as before] … if,
Bhāradvāja, a person has acceptance based on contemplation of views;
‘Such is my view, my reflection, and my acceptance’—by speaking thus, one protects the truth, yet one does not yet reach a definitive conclusion with absolute certainty:
‘This alone is the truth; all else is false.’
"To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is the preservation of truth; to this extent one preserves truth; and to this extent we prescribe the preservation of truth.
But to this extent, there is as yet no awakening to truth.
"To this extent, Master Gotama, there is the preservation of truth; to this extent one preserves truth; and to this extent we perceive the preservation of truth."
"But to what extent, Master Gotama, is there the awakening to truth? To what extent does one awaken to truth?
We ask Master Gotama about the awakening to truth.
"In this case, Bhāradvāja, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.
A householder or a householder’s son, having approached him, examines him with respect to three things:
things that provoke lust, things that provoke hatred, and things that provoke delusion.
He considers: "Does this venerable one possess such lust-provoking qualities that, his mind being overwhelmed by such lust-provoking qualities, he might speak what he does not know?"
"Does he know 'I know' while not seeing, or say 'I see' while not seeing,
or encourage another toward that purpose which would lead to the long-term harm and suffering of others?
Examining him, he knows this:
‘This venerable one does not possess such alluring things that, with his mind obsessed by such alluring things,

he might speak of what he has not known as “I know,” or speak of what he has not seen as “I see,” or might incite another to act for their sake, which would lead to the long-term harm and suffering of others.’
"Indeed, such is this venerable one’s conduct of body and such his conduct of speech as that of one who is free from greed.

Furthermore, the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise;
that Dhamma cannot be easily taught by one who is greedy."
When, while investigating him, he perceives that he is pure regarding qualities that provoke lust, he investigates him further regarding qualities that provoke hatred:
"Does this venerable one possess such qualities that provoke hatred that, his mind obsessed by them, he might say 'I know' when he does not know,
or say 'I see' when he does not see?"
‘I see it,’ or would he encourage another for that purpose, thinking, ‘This will lead to the long-term harm and suffering of others’?
Examining him, he knows this:
‘There are no such corruptible qualities in this venerable one by which his mind might be overwhelmed so that he would speak without knowing.’
One might say "I know" when one does not see,
or say "I see" when one does not know, or incite another to that end, which would lead to the long-term harm and suffering of others.
Yet such is this venerable one’s conduct of body and such his conduct of speech that it is as if he were free from malice.

"Furthermore, the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise;
that Dhamma cannot be easily taught by one who is corrupted.
When, upon investigation, he perceives him to be pure regarding those qualities that lead to corruption, he then investigates him further regarding those qualities that lead to delusion.
"Is there such a state of delusion in this venerable one, by which his mind is so overwhelmed that, not knowing,
he might say 'I know,' or not seeing,
he might say 'I see,' or he might incite another to do something that would lead to their long-term harm and suffering?"
Investigating him, he knows this:
"This venerable one does not possess such qualities that lead to delusion by which, his mind being overwhelmed, he might say 'I know' when he does not know,
or say 'I see' when he does not see."
"I see," or he might encourage another for that purpose, which would lead to the long-term harm and suffering of others.
Yet such is this venerable one’s conduct of body and such his conduct of speech as that of one who is not deluded.

Furthermore, the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, difficult to awaken to, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
"That Dhamma cannot be well taught by one who is deluded.
When, upon investigation, he perceives that [the teacher] is purified of the qualities that lead to delusion, then he places his faith in him;
having conceived faith, he approaches him; approaching, he pays respectful homage.
While attending upon [the teacher], he lends an ear; with an attentive ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he retains it;

he examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained; as he examines the meaning, the teachings become acceptable through reflection; when there is acceptance through reflection on the teachings, zeal arises;
being zealous, he exerts himself; exerting himself, he investigates; having investigated, he strives; thus, with his self dedicated [to the goal].
Being thus concentrated, one realizes the ultimate truth with the body and, having penetrated it through wisdom, sees it.
To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is the awakening to truth; to this extent one awakens to truth; and to this extent we describe the awakening to truth;
yet to this extent, there is as yet no full attainment of truth.
“In this much, Master Gotama, is there the awakening to truth; in this much does one awaken to truth; and in this much do we perceive the awakening to truth.
But in what measure, Master Gotama, is there the attainment of truth; in what measure does one attain truth? We ask Master Gotama about the attainment of truth.”
“Bhāradvāja, it is through the cultivation, development, and frequent practice of those very same phenomena that there is the realization of truth.
To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is the realization of truth; to this extent one attains the truth; and to this extent we proclaim the realization of truth.
“To this extent, Master Gotama, there is the realization of truth; to this extent one attains the truth; and to this extent we perceive the realization of truth.”
"But for the realization of truth, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is most helpful for the realization of truth.
"For the realization of truth, Bhāradvāja, striving is most helpful."
If one were not to exert effort, one would not reach truth.
But because one exerts effort, one reaches truth.
Therefore, exertion for the attainment of truth is of great benefit.
“But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for striving?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is most helpful for striving.
“Bhāradvāja, comparison is most helpful for striving.”
"One should not weigh this; one should not strive for this.
But because one weighs it, therefore one strives.
Therefore, weighing is of great benefit to striving."
“But for weighing, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for weighing.
“For weighing, Bhāradvāja, effort is most helpful.”
"One would not strive for this, nor would one weigh it up.
But because one strives, therefore one weighs it up.
Therefore, striving is of great benefit for weighing things up."
“But, Master Gotama, what thing is helpful for exertion?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is helpful for exertion.
“Bhāradvāja, zeal is helpful for exertion.”
If this desire did not arise, one would not exert oneself;
but because desire arises, one exerts oneself.
Therefore, desire is of great benefit to exertion.”
“But, Master Gotama, what thing is of great service to desire?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is of great service to desire.
“Bhāradvāja, for desire, the acceptance of the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*) is of great service.”
If these phenomena did not withstand contemplation, this desire would not arise.
But because these phenomena do withstand contemplation, therefore desire arises.
Therefore, the acceptance of phenomena through contemplation is highly beneficial for desire.”
“But, Master Gotama, what is helpful for the patient acceptance that comes from reflecting on the Dhamma?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is helpful for the patient acceptance that comes from reflecting on the Dhamma.
“For the patient acceptance that comes from reflecting on the Dhamma, Bhāradvāja, the investigation of the meaning is helpful.”
If one were not to examine the meaning, these teachings would not be able to withstand reflective contemplation.

But because one examines the meaning, these teachings are able to withstand reflective contemplation. Therefore, the examination of the meaning is of great benefit for the reflective acceptance of the teachings.”
“But for the investigation of the meaning, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for the investigation of the meaning.
“For the investigation of the meaning, Bhāradvāja, the retention of the Dhamma is most helpful.”
"One would not retain this Dhamma, nor would one examine its meaning.
But because one retains the Dhamma, one examines its meaning.
Therefore, the retention of the Dhamma is of great benefit for the examination of its meaning."
“But for the purpose of retaining the Dhamma, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is most helpful for retaining the Dhamma.
“For the purpose of retaining the Dhamma, Bhāradvāja, listening to the Dhamma is most helpful.”
One would not hear this Dhamma, nor would one retain this Dhamma.
But because one hears the Dhamma, one retains the Dhamma.
Therefore, hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit for the retention of the Dhamma.
“But what, Master Gotama, is the quality that is most helpful for hearing the Dhamma?
We ask Master Gotama about the quality that is most helpful for hearing the Dhamma.
“Bhāradvāja, giving ear is the quality most helpful for hearing the Dhamma.”
One would not lend an ear to this, nor would one hear this Dhamma.
But because one lends an ear, one hears the Dhamma.
Therefore, lending an ear to hear the Dhamma is of great benefit.”
“But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for giving ear?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is most helpful for giving ear.
“Attending upon [a teacher], Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for giving ear.”
One would not attend upon this if one were not to lend an ear to it;
but because one attends upon it, one lends an ear to it.
Therefore, attending upon is of great benefit for lending an ear.”
“But for the purpose of attending upon him, Master Gotama, what quality is most helpful?
We ask Master Gotama about the quality that is most helpful for attending upon him.
“For attending upon him, Bhāradvāja, approaching him is most helpful.”
One would not approach this person, nor would one attend upon them.
But because one approaches them, therefore one attends upon them.
Therefore, approaching is of great benefit for attending upon."
“But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for approaching?
We ask Master Gotama about the thing that is most helpful for approaching.
“Bhāradvāja, faith is most helpful for approaching.”
Faith would not arise in one who did not approach;
one does not approach because faith arises.
Therefore, faith is of great benefit for approaching.”
“We asked Master Gotama about the preservation of truth, and Master Gotama has explained the preservation of truth to us;
that is both pleasing and acceptable to us, and we are satisfied with it.
We asked Master Gotama about the awakening to truth, and Master Gotama has explained the awakening to truth to us.”
And that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us, and therefore we are satisfied.
We asked Master Gotama about the realization of truth, and Master Gotama has explained the realization of truth;
and that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us, and therefore we are satisfied.
We asked Master Gotama about the Dhamma that is helpful for the realization of truth, and Master Gotama has explained the Dhamma that is helpful for the realization of truth;
we approve of it and accept it, and therefore we are satisfied.
Whatever we asked Master Gotama, all that Master Gotama has answered.
And that is both pleasing and acceptable to us, and for that reason we are delighted.
For previously, Master Gotama, we thought thus:
"Who are these shavelings, these wretched little ascetics, these outcasts, the dark offspring of our kinsmen? Who are they that understand the Dhamma?"?
"Truly, Master Gotama has generated in me love for the recluses, confidence in the recluses, and respect for the recluses.
Excellent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
The Caṅkīsutta, the fifth, is finished.
